newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Diplomatic ballet underlines West's Africa failure.
newsitem.headline: Diplomatic ballet underlines West's Africa failure.

text.p: A "diplomatic ballet" in the West while eastern Zaire slips into bloody chaos underlines the international community's failure to devise a strategy for Africa, by far the world's poorest continent.

Political analysts and regional experts say Europe's governments, faced with a potential crisis in central Africa of immense political and economic implications, are virtually bereft of ideas on how to deal with their old colonies.

"Different ambassadors, different embassies have been going backwards and forwards to Rwanda, but what do they do? What progress is made?" says Rwanda's ambassador to Belgium, Manzi Bakuramatusa. "This diplomatic ballet is not the answer."

Independent analysts concur, saying that faced with crises across the African continent, Europe's main answer is to summon discredited regional leaders to peace conferences and hold a sequence of meetings seemingly out of touch with reality.

They argue that over the last 30 years, the West has gradually washed its hands of Africa. As the continent moved from colonisation to marginalisation, virtually every problem was treated as a product of poverty alone.

"People will never comprehend Africa's crisis so long as they continue to assume it is mainly an economic one," said Adebayo Adedeji, the Nigerian economist and former U.N. Africa head, in a recent interview.
"Africa is primarily a political crisis with devastating economic consequences," he added.

The process of disengagement has been accelerated by the end of the Cold War and the dismantling of apartheid in South Africa -- the one area where the United States, prompted by the powerful black lobby, showed real interest.

Last year, the 47 countries of sub-Saharan Africa attracted a mere three percent of the flow of foreign direct investment into the developing world compared with almost 60 percent in East Asia and the Pacific.

Consequently, while bloated bodies once more this week floated down the rivers that feed the Great Lakes area, European diplomats discussed help for elections few believe will ever take place and food for abandoned refugee camps.

But nothing, analysts and regional diplomats say, demonstrates the paucity of any genuine ideas of how to deal with the continent than the decision to try to call on the Organisation of African Unity (OAU) to take responsibility.

"There should be a force to monitor and protect refugees. This should be from the OAU with logistical support from the EU," said Joan Burton, the Irish minister of state for overseas aid, voicing the view now most popular within EU circles.

Burton, whose country holds the rotating EU presidency, said she hoped an outline agreement on this as well as a ceasefire between all parties in the area would be agreed at a planned regional summit in coming days.
The idea is has foundered in the past over basic questions such as which countries would or could contribute forces and how they could enforce a ceasefire without inflaming the sitation.

For years, the pan-African body -- created in the heady days of post-colonial independence -- has been unable to meet the challenges posed by decades of economic mismanagement, dictatorial rule, corruption and foreign exploitation.

"It is pathetic...the OAU? What are these people talking about? Nigerian troops policing Zaire, what a wonderful idea. The OAU is a complete irrelevance that cannot even pay its heating bills," said one African analyst.

Bakuramatusa and other African diplomats have urged international action to deal with the deteriorating crisis, where Zaire and Rwanda are slipping towards war, but said the crisis must not be treated simply as a humanitarian problem.

Bakuramatusa attacked the EU's aid chief Emma Bonino for calling for humanitarian corridors to the teeming refugee camps on the borders with Burundi and Rwanda, now home to several of the perpetrators of the 1994 genocide of mainly Tutsi Rwandans.
Rwanda says the U.N. has clothed and fed the very people its own war crimes' tribunal is seeking, fuelling resentment and the potential for more conflict.
"But who expresses concern about that?," Bakuramatusa added.

Belgian Foreign Minister Eric Derycke said the country would host an international conference on the crisis and try to act as the "motor" in efforts to draw up a solution, but ruled out the despatch of any troops to the region.
Derycke said he supported an OAU initiative while French President Jacques Chirac urged heads of east and central African states to call a conference.
